metadata.file_name: 173. Mang et al. (2021). The influence of ICT use and related attitudes on students’ math and science performance: multilevel analyses of the last decade’s PISA survey.pdf
metadata.title: The influence of ICT use and related attitudes on students’ math and science performance: multilevel analyses of the last decade’s PISA survey

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 sampling structures to motivate and evaluate how to incorporate two-stage school→student sampling weights in two-level hierarchical models (students nested in schools). The authors describe final student weights as products of school base weights and student base weights with non-response adjustments, and they explicitly compare multiple weighting scenarios (e.g., no weights, unscaled weights, only student weights, only school weights, and several scaling rules for level-one/student weights). For the recommended approach, they use only level-two school weights (final school weights) in the multilevel models, while omitting level-one/student weights; this is argued to avoid bias in intercept and variance components when school selection probabilities differ. The paper does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife) as part of the simulation; instead it focuses on pseudo maximum likelihood estimation with sandwich-type variance estimation implemented by Mplus and SAS.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for the PISA 2015 application or the simulation beyond non-response adjustments used to construct sampling weights. Because the dependent variable is treated as PISA competence approximated by a plausible value (first PV) in the application, the manuscript does not provide a transparent missingness strategy for item nonresponse or PV-related missingness. This represents a reporting gap for missing-data treatment in the analytic pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The simulation population is based on the German PISA 2015 sampling frame and German PISA 2015 sample characteristics; 1000 Monte Carlo sample replications are drawn from this German population. Each replication draws 234 schools with a maximum of 25 students per school (and in schools with fewer than 25 eligible students, all eligible students are selected). For the real-data application, the authors apply the recommended weighting approach to PISA 2015 data (science domain) using the first plausible value and ESCS at both student and school levels; the manuscript does not specify additional analytic exclusions beyond the weighting/non-response structure.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (Germany) Science competence (first plausible value), two-level MLM (students within schools)
main_findings.target_variable: Intercept (β0) and variance components (σ²ε within schools; σ²τ between schools) under different sampling-weighting schemes
top_predictors: Only school weights vs other weighting/scaling approaches
main_findings.performance_metrics: Empirical 95% coverage rates (CR) across 1000 Monte Carlo replications; key result: Only School Weights, Scaled Weights: Cluster, and Scaled Weights: ECluster provide least-biased and sufficiently precise parameter estimates across all three simulation scenarios. In Scenario 1 (PISA-like ICC=0.52), Only School Weights yields CR≈1.00 for β0 and β1 and ≈0.95 for β2 (SAS/Mplus tables), while several alternatives show CR≈0.00 for β0. In the PISA 2015 application, Only School Weights is used as reference; alternative weighting schemes produce higher intercept estimates (overestimation) and can underestimate variance components.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (Germany) science competence data in two-level hierarchical models, the study compared multiple sampling-weighting schemes and found that using only level-two school weights (with no level-one/student weights) yields the least biased and sufficiently precise estimates of the intercept and variance components, while alternatives (e.g., only student weights, unscaled/final student weights, and some scaling variants) can substantially distort parameters. This indicates that multilevel analyses of PISA-style two-stage samples should prioritize final school weights at the school level to preserve validity of between-school and within-school inferences, though the study is based on simulation-based evaluation rather than causal identification.

data.outcome_summary: This paper evaluates how to scale and apply PISA sampling weights in two-level multilevel models (students nested in schools) using pseudo maximum likelihood estimation with sandwich-type standard errors. It runs a Monte Carlo simulation with 1000 replications for three scenarios that vary between-school intraclass correlation (ICC=0.52, 0.05, 0.79) and compares nine weighting approaches implemented in Mplus (default two-level settings) and SAS (PROC GLIMMIX with adaptive quadrature). Across scenarios, the weighting schemes Only School Weights, Scaled Weights: Cluster, and Scaled Weights: ECluster show the best performance in recovering true population parameters, with Only School Weights recommended for ease of implementation. In the PISA 2015 application (science domain; first PV; ESCS at student and school levels), non-recommended weighting approaches tend to overestimate the intercept and can underestimate variance components. The study does not provide a detailed missing-data handling strategy for the PV-based outcome, so validity depends on the assumed weight/PV framework rather than a fully documented missingness pipeline.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript is primarily a simulation-and-methods comparison paper focused on weighting and estimation procedures in multilevel modeling rather than training predictive machine-learning models. As a result, there is no ML algorithmic target/prediction pipeline to extract (ml_techniques is empty), and the main empirical outputs are coverage rates and parameter recovery for hierarchical model components. The paper also does not report a conventional missing-data handling method for the PV-based outcome, which is why missing_data_handling is set to not_reported.
